title: Offshore Topsides and Deck Structures
analyses: Global and local finite-element stress analysis
Deck plate, beam, column and framing analysis
Equipment support and machinery foundation analysis
Crane pedestal and lifting support analysis
Module support, skid and grillage analysis
Blast, fire and accidental load structural response analysis

models.text: The suite should implement static equilibrium equations, Cauchy elasticity, generalized Hooke's law, Euler–Bernoulli and Timoshenko beam theories, Kirchhoff–Love plate theory, Mindlin–Reissner plate theory, classical shell theory, grillage analysis, moment distribution methods, slope-deflection methods, matrix stiffness formulations, shear deformation relationships, Saint-Venant torsion, elastic beam-column analysis, Euler buckling, lateral–torsional buckling, plate buckling and frame stability analysis.

The suite should incorporate von Mises plasticity, Tresca yield theory, isotropic hardening, kinematic hardening, geometric stiffness formulations, second-order structural analysis, P–Delta and P–delta effects, nonlinear connection stiffness models, contact mechanics, bolted joint slip models, weld stress concentration models, plastic-hinge formulations and large-deflection plate and shell analysis.

Dynamic calculations should use Newton's second law, Lagrange's equations of motion, mass–stiffness–damping formulations, modal superposition, eigenvalue analysis, forced harmonic response, transient dynamic analysis, frequency response functions, Campbell diagrams, rotor unbalance forcing models, machinery foundation impedance models, vibration isolation relationships, damping identification and fatigue vibration models.

The suite should include pressure–impulse diagram methods, single-degree-of-freedom blast response models, multi-degree-of-freedom dynamic models, explicit nonlinear dynamic finite-element methods, strain-rate-dependent material models such as Johnson–Cook where appropriate, thermal conduction equations, transient heat-transfer models, temperature-dependent material degradation, thermal expansion stress models, plastic collapse and progressive failure simulations.

Applicable methods include quasi-static lifting analysis, dynamic amplification approaches, multi-point support stiffness analysis, transportation acceleration models, seafastening force equilibrium, structural fatigue models, fracture mechanics, residual strength assessment and nonlinear load redistribution.

The suite should combine global beam-element structural models with detailed shell and solid finite-element models, machinery dynamics with structural response, CFD-generated blast loads with nonlinear structural response, transient thermal modelling with temperature-dependent structural mechanics, and Bayesian inspection updating with fatigue-life forecasting. Reduced-order models and calibrated response surfaces may be used for repeated load-case assessment after comparison with appropriate high-fidelity calculations.

inputs.text: Deck dimensions, number of levels, deck elevations, structural grids, beam spans, column positions, plate dimensions, openings, stiffeners and connection details.
Beam profiles, column cross-sections, channel sections, hollow sections, plate thicknesses, connection geometry and weld sizes.
Structural steel grades, elastic properties, strength limits, density, toughness and thermal expansion characteristics.
Vessel and separator weights, compressors, generators, pumps, storage vessels, process modules, pipe racks and electrical equipment weights.
Live loads, maintenance loads, platform occupancy loads, storage loads, temporary construction loads and equipment operating loads.
Rotational speeds, forcing frequencies, unbalanced forces, startup/shutdown speeds, equipment inertia and machinery support stiffness.
Crane pedestal geometry, rated lifting loads, boom radius, overturning moments, lifting configurations and dynamic amplification factors.
Skid dimensions, structural support points, module centre of gravity, equipment load distribution and grillage stiffness.
Wind pressure distributions, wave-induced support accelerations, vessel-induced motions and site-specific seismic parameters.
Blast overpressure-time curves, explosion locations, fire temperature-time profiles, impact energies and accidental load combinations.
Jacket interface stiffness, deck leg restraint conditions, support displacement limits and connection characteristics.
Weld classifications, cyclic loading history, corrosion records, crack measurements and maintenance records.
Lift point coordinates, rigging geometry, transportation accelerations, temporary support positions and seafastening loads.
Allowable deflections, vibration limits, design life, strength criteria, fire resistance requirements and applicable load combinations.

subtitle: Deck framing, modules, equipment supports, vibration, lifting, accidental loading and topside-to-jacket load transfer.
ic: The initial conditions shall define the topside structural configuration, including deck plates, beams, columns, bracing systems, module supports, crane pedestals, machinery foundations, pipe racks and major equipment supports. The initial material conditions shall include structural steel properties, concrete properties where applicable, plate thicknesses, section geometry and joint characteristics.

The initial static condition shall ordinarily represent the topside under its own weight and installed permanent equipment before variable operating loads are imposed. For in-place analyses, the starting equilibrium shall include sustained loads and the support reactions or movements transmitted from the supporting jacket or floating facility.

For equipment foundation analysis, the initial machine state may be stationary, with defined rotor positions, equipment mass distribution and support stiffness. Dynamic analyses shall begin with specified displacement, velocity and equipment operating conditions.

For blast, fire and accidental loading analysis, the initial conditions shall establish pre-event member temperatures, structural stresses, material condition and existing deflections. Existing topsides shall include recorded corrosion damage, fatigue deterioration, connection defects and previous structural modifications where relevant.
bc: Support boundary conditions shall represent the connections between the topside and jacket, hull, columns or other foundation structure. These may include rigid restraints, elastic support stiffness, imposed displacements, support rotations and foundation reaction characteristics.

Structural load boundaries shall apply equipment weights, process loads, personnel loading, storage loading, crane loads, pipe-support reactions and machinery forces at their actual contact or connection locations. Plate, beam and connection boundaries shall preserve the intended load transfer and structural continuity.

Dynamic boundary conditions shall prescribe machinery excitation frequencies, rotating-equipment forces, support motions and structural damping. Wind and seismic boundary conditions shall apply the appropriate distributed aerodynamic loads and ground-motion effects.

For blast analysis, pressure-time histories shall be applied to exposed structural surfaces. For fire analysis, exposed member surfaces shall receive appropriate temperature or heat-transfer conditions. During transportation and lifting, temporary support conditions, lifting-point forces, rigging restraints and imposed vessel accelerations shall be represented. Fatigue evaluations shall use the relevant fluctuating loads at the structural interfaces.

calibration: Calibration should use structural strain measurements, deck deflection surveys, machinery vibration recordings, modal testing, equipment foundation measurements and field inspection records. Structural joint stiffness, support flexibility and damping should be calibrated against measured dynamic and static responses.

Machinery foundation models should use measured excitation frequencies, operating forces, dynamic stiffness and vibration amplitudes. Equipment manufacturers' certified data should be used wherever available, with field measurements providing additional calibration evidence.
Deck plate, beam, column and framing assumptions should be calibrated using material coupon tests, structural load tests and measured deformation of representative components.

Blast loading parameters should be informed by controlled explosion experiments, validated pressure measurements and representative industrial test data. Fire response parameters, including thermal boundary conditions and temperature-dependent material properties, should be informed by furnace tests, fire exposure measurements and documented fire-resistance experiments.
Fatigue parameters should be calibrated using representative welded connection tests, measured cyclic stresses and appropriate structural detail fatigue datasets.

Where topside structures are supported by jackets, interface stiffness and reaction-transfer assumptions should be calibrated using measured support response and operational load information where available.
verification: Structural verification should include analytical beam, plate, shell, frame and connection benchmarks covering bending, shear, axial loading, torsion, buckling and deformation.
Finite-element mesh convergence should be performed for global framing, local plate bending, equipment support regions, connection details, crane pedestals and structural discontinuities.

Static equilibrium checks should confirm consistency among applied loads, member forces and support reactions. Structural compatibility and load transfer should be tested across deck modules, skids, grillages and supporting structures.

Modal analysis should be verified using simple systems with known natural frequencies and benchmark multi-degree-of-freedom structural models. Dynamic analyses should undergo time-step convergence, damping verification and excitation-frequency sensitivity testing.

Buckling calculations should be checked against established column, plate and shell instability benchmarks. Nonlinear post-buckling analyses should include load-step and imperfection sensitivity studies.

Blast and fire calculations should be verified through pressure application tests, transient structural benchmarks, thermal conduction benchmarks, temperature-dependent material implementation checks and coupled thermal-structural response tests.

Lifting, transportation and installation cases should be checked for support equilibrium, load distribution, reaction compatibility and consistency between temporary and permanent structural configurations.
validation: Static deck response should be validated using measured strains, support reactions and deflections from representative load tests or operating structures.
Predicted machinery vibration frequencies and amplitudes should be compared against independent measurements from equipment operating under known loading conditions.
Crane pedestal response should be compared with instrumented load testing, certified crane loading cases and measured structural deformation where available.
Blast and fire structural predictions should be validated using controlled experimental datasets that report pressure, temperature, deformation and observed structural damage.
Fatigue predictions should be assessed using independent welded-detail fatigue tests and long-term inspection records.
Transportation and installation predictions should be compared with measured acceleration histories, sling loads, support reactions and structural movements.
Validation should assess both local and global response, ensuring that agreement in overall displacement does not conceal unacceptable errors in local stress or connection behaviour.

geometry.text: Topsides modules, deck plates, structural beams, columns, bracing, machinery foundations, equipment skids, lifting frames, crane pedestals, pipe racks and welded structural connections.

geometry.cat: Conventional and universal CAD geometry formats
geometry.text: STEP (.step, .stp), IGES (.iges, .igs), Parasolid (.x_t, .x_b), ACIS (.sat, .sab), IFC (.ifc), DXF (.dxf) and supported DWG (.dwg) should be accepted for the geometry of individual members, equipment supports, plates, bolted connections, structural assemblies and fabrication details.

SDNF, CIS/2, IFC, ISO 15926-based plant information exchanges where geometry mappings are available, and compatible structural node/member XML, JSON and CSV representations should be supported. Plant-specific proprietary assembly formats may also be accepted through dedicated translators, allowing equipment foundations, lifting structures and process module geometry to be assembled into a common structural model.
Nastran BDF/NAS, Abaqus INP, ANSYS CDB, Gmsh MSH, MED, UNV, VTK/VTU and Exodus should be supported for imported beam, shell and solid meshes, including localized plate and weld-region models.

STL, OBJ, PLY, GLB, E57, LAS/LAZ and point-cloud XYZ data should be accepted for digitized equipment layouts, legacy topsides, retrofits and as-built scanning. Imported scans should pass geometry reconstruction and dimensional checks before being used for structural verification.
